| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*erasespamedcomments*" OR (Web.url="*clean=yes*" AND Web.url="*suppr*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count>=1
YesWiki CVE-2026-52766 exploit request — erasespamedcomments clean=yes suppr[] POST AIExploitation Medium
Detects the exploitation POST for CVE-2026-52766 in WAF/web request logs: a POST carrying the erasespamedcomments action together with the clean=yes flag and a suppr[] array. Requires request-body inspection on the WAF (the parameters live in the POST body, not the URL query string). Rationale: Keys on the three attacker-controlled strings from the article PoC (erasespamedcomments action name, clean=yes flag, suppr[] array); the combination is not produced by normal wiki browsing/editing. Confidence is Medium because the params sit in the POST body, so it only fires where the WAF logs request bodies. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52766/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An authorized moderator legitimately running the erasespamedcomments spam-cleanup action against genuine spam pages
  • WAF/vulnerability scanners (Nuclei, Burp) probing for CVE-2026-52766 in an authorized pentest
  • Security team validating the 4.6.6 patch with a benign reproduction request
  • Log-replay or SIEM test harness re-ingesting the PoC payload
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the suppr[] tags in the body to see which pages were targeted (PagePrincipale = front page) and check the response code/size to gauge success; verify the source IP is not an authorized admin. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and add a WAF rule denying POSTs containing clean=yes+suppr[] to unauthenticated sessions; upgrade YesWiki to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: correlate with Syslog 'Suppression de la page' entries within 60s to confirm pages were actually deleted, and review the same IP for other YesWiki CVEs from this advisory batch (SQLi, SSRF, eval RCE).
CommonSecurityLog

| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "erasespamedcomments"
    or Message has "erasespamedcomments"
    or (Message has "clean=yes" and Message has "suppr")
    or (RequestURL has "clean=yes" and RequestURL has "suppr")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New GigaWiper Windows Backdoor Bundles Disk Wiping, Fake Ransomware, and Spyware

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 15 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has taken apart a destructive Windows backdoor it calls GigaWiper. What stands out is how it is built: not one tool but three older destructive programs bolted into one, offered as commands the operator can choose from. Each is a different way to break a machine: wipe the whole disk, overwrite the Windows drive, or run fake "ransomware" that scrambles files with a key it never saves

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — New GigaWiper Windows Backdoor Bundles Disk Wiping, Fake Ransomware, and Spyware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GigaWiper 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task firing every minute · [LLM] GigaWiper self-tracking registry key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GigaWiper firewall rule masquerading as Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost · [LLM] GigaWiper C2 over RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO or known command servers from endpoints · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] takeown/icacls seizing ownership of Windows boot files (bootmgr, ntoskrnl.exe) · [LLM] GigaWiper fake ransomware: mass '.candy' file writes and wallpaper swap · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GigaWiper 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task firing every minute AIInstallation High
Hunts GigaWiper/BLUERABBIT persistence: a scheduled task masquerading as 'OneDrive Update' created with a one-minute repeat interval via schtasks.exe. Legitimate OneDrive updater tasks never run every minute, making the minute cadence the high-fidelity tell. Rationale: Uses the article's exact task name 'OneDrive Update' plus the one-minute (/sc minute /mo 1) trigger, which is the differentiator from Microsoft's legit OneDrive updater tasks. Corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT write-up describing the same persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise RMM/GPO deploying a genuinely-named OneDrive maintenance task (rare, and not at 1-minute cadence)
  • Admin manually testing schtasks with a 'OneDrive' string in a lab
  • Software packaging tools (PDQ, SCCM) creating high-frequency check-in tasks that coincidentally reference OneDrive
  • Third-party backup agents that re-register OneDrive sync tasks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks command line and the task XML (schtasks /query /tn "OneDrive Update" /xml); confirm the action points to a non-Microsoft binary outside %ProgramFiles%\Microsoft OneDrive. 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host in Defender, and snapshot memory before reboot (wiper may trigger on reboot). 3) Hunt: pivot on the task's action binary hash across the fleet, check HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment (UC2) and the Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost firewall rule (UC3) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "OneDrive Update"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("minute", "/mo 1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "OneDrive Update"
| where CommandLine has_any ("minute", "/mo 1")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: GigaWiper OneDrive Update Scheduled Task Every Minute
id: 3f2b9c14-8a71-4d0e-9c2a-5b7e1f0a9d34
description: Detects creation of a scheduled task masquerading as 'OneDrive Update' with a one-minute repeat interval, matching GigaWiper/BLUERABBIT persistence.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gigawiper-windows-backdoor-bundles.html
  - https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'OneDrive Update'
      - 'minute'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\\Schtasks.exe) @CommandLine:*OneDrive*Update* @CommandLine:(*minute* OR *MINUTE* OR *Minute*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i CommandLine=/OneDrive Update/i CommandLine=/minute/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

GigaWiper self-tracking registry key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment AIInstallation High
Hunts the GigaWiper masquerade artifact: a value written under HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment (note: NOT the legitimate HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive path) used by the implant to track itself while posing as OneDrive. Rationale: Uses the exact article-named key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment and explicitly excludes the real HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive path, so the only hits are the implant's masquerade. Falcon FDR AsepValueUpdate only covers autostart keys, so this non-ASEP key is left empty for LogScale. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://gbhackers.com/bluerabbit-backdoor-encrypts-files/
ATT&CKT1112 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party tool coincidentally creating an 'OneDrive\Environment' subkey (uncommon)
  • Backup/migration tooling cloning HKCU hives between profiles
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in an instrumented VM
  • Manual regedit exploration during IR of an already-known host
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the value data under the key and the InitiatingProcess that wrote it; the writing process is the implant. 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the process binary (hash it against the four GigaWiper SHA256s) before any reboot to avoid triggering the wiper. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same key and cross-reference hosts also showing the 'OneDrive Update' minute task (UC1) and outbound RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO to the C2 IPs (UC5).
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"OneDrive\Environment"
| where RegistryKey !has @"Microsoft\OneDrive"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "onedrive.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"OneDrive\Environment"
| where RegistryKey !has @"Microsoft\OneDrive"
| where ActingProcessName !has "onedrive.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

GigaWiper firewall rule masquerading as Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost AICommand & Control High
Hunts GigaWiper opening its remote-control (hidden VNC) channel by adding an inbound Windows Firewall rule named after a real component, Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost, via netsh advfirewall or New-NetFirewallRule. Rationale: Uses the exact firewall-rule masquerade name Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost from the article; that real component never legitimately requires an operator-added inbound netsh/PowerShell firewall rule, making command-line references high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gigawiper-windows-backdoor-bundles.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1562.004 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint management tooling scripting firewall rules that reference CloudExperienceHost by coincidence (very rare)
  • IT admin troubleshooting OOBE/CloudExperienceHost connectivity manually
  • Security baseline/GPO hardening scripts touching CloudExperienceHost
  • Custom imaging scripts adding named firewall exceptions
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the new firewall rule (netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name=Microsoft.Windows.CloudExperienceHost) and identify the local port it opens and the binary bound to it. 2) Contain: delete the rule, block inbound at network layer, and isolate the host; the rule fronts a VNC/remote-control channel. 3) Hunt: look for listening sockets and inbound connections from the C2 IPs 185.182.193.21 / 212.8.248.104, plus co-occurring UC1/UC2 artifacts on the host.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "CloudExperienceHost"
| where (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "advfirewall" and ProcessCommandLine has "add")
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "New-NetFirewallRule")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4688

     or (NewProcessName has "powershell" and CommandLine has "New-NetFirewallRule")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

takeown/icacls seizing ownership of Windows boot files (bootmgr, ntoskrnl.exe) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the GigaWiper pre-destruction step: takeown.exe and icacls.exe used to seize ownership/ACLs of boot-critical files such as bootmgr and ntoskrnl.exe, a strong precursor to the raw-disk/Windows-drive wipers. Rationale: Directly implements the article's stated defender signal: takeown/icacls taking ownership of bootmgr and ntoskrnl.exe outside maintenance windows. Ownership seizure of boot files by these LOLBins is almost never legitimate on endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gigawiper-windows-backdoor-bundles.html • https://gbhackers.com/bluerabbit-backdoor-encrypts-files/
ATT&CKT1222.001 T1561.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate boot-repair (bcdedit/DISM/sfc) sessions during OS servicing where an admin scripts takeown on boot files
  • Dual-boot or imaging engineers adjusting boot-file ACLs
  • In-place Windows feature-update rollback touching bootmgr
  • Forensic tooling normalizing permissions on a mounted image
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe","dism.exe","tiworker.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm this is outside a change/maintenance window and identify the initiating process/user; boot-file ownership changes on a workstation are almost always malicious. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host and do NOT reboot (wipers commonly trigger on reboot); capture a disk/memory image. 3) Hunt: search the same host and peers for raw disk-write handles (\\.\PhysicalDrive), event-log clearing (wevtutil cl), and the C2 IPs; treat any host with this signal as pre-detonation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("takeown.exe","icacls.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bootmgr","ntoskrnl.exe","bootmgfw")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\takeown.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\icacls.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("bootmgr","ntoskrnl.exe","bootmgfw")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

GigaWiper C2 over RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO or known command servers from endpoints AICommand & Control High
Hunts GigaWiper command traffic that rides legitimate services (RabbitMQ 5672 tasking, Redis 6379 results, MinIO 9000 exfil) to public IPs, or any connection to the two named command servers 185.182.193.21 and 212.8.248.104. Rationale: Combines the two article/vendor-confirmed C2 IPs (high-fidelity, any port) with the RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO port set restricted to public destinations, matching the article's 'RabbitMQ or Redis traffic from ordinary desktops rather than servers.' IPs corroborated by Binary Defense (same command servers as BLUERABBIT). Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1071 T1567 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/DevOps workstations legitimately connecting to a cloud-hosted RabbitMQ/Redis/MinIO (5672/6379/9000) over the internet
  • Managed message-broker SaaS (CloudAMQP, Redis Enterprise Cloud, self-hosted MinIO on a public VPS)
  • CI runners on desktops pulling artifacts from a public MinIO bucket
  • Monitoring agents polling a public Redis endpoint
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\\Users\\", @"\\Windows\\Temp\\", @"\\AppData\\") or RemoteIP in ("185.182.193.21","212.8.248.104")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process; a broker/store client (or a Go binary in a temp/user path) on a non-server desktop reaching these ports/IPs is suspicious. Connections to 185.182.193.21/212.8.248.104 are alert-worthy regardless of port. 2) Contain: block both C2 IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and preserve state before reboot. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internal hosts touching those IPs/ports, correlate with UC1–UC4 host artifacts, and check MinIO (9000) sessions for outbound exfil volume.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("185.182.193.21","212.8.248.104")
     or (RemotePort in (5672,6379,9000) and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("185.182.193.21","212.8.248.104")
     or (DstPortNumber in (5672,6379,9000) and DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber) by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc

GigaWiper fake ransomware: mass '.candy' file writes and wallpaper swap AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Crucio-derived fake-ransomware module: bulk creation/rename of files with the .candy extension on a single host (no ransom note, no recoverable key), optionally paired with a desktop wallpaper change to an alarming warning image. Rationale: Uses the article's exact .candy extension left by the Crucio-based fake-ransomware module, with a per-host volume threshold (>=25) to separate a mass-encryption event from an isolated filename. Corroborated by Binary Defense/BLUERABBIT reporting the same encrypt-then-wipe behavior. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-bluerabbit-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1486 T1491.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche application legitimately using a .candy file extension for its own data (rare)
  • Malware researcher replaying the sample in a sandbox
  • Backup software creating many files that a naming scheme coincidentally suffixes with .candy
  • A single user renaming a handful of files (filtered by the >=25 threshold)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess writing .candy files and its hash; because the key is never saved, treat this as destruction, not recoverable ransomware. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and pull it offline before it pivots to the disk/Windows-drive wipers; preserve a forensic image. 3) Hunt: check the host for wallpaper changes (HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop\Wallpaper), event-log clearing, and the boot-file takeown/icacls (UC4); sweep peers for the four GigaWiper SHA256 hashes and the C2 IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".candy"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), FileCount=dcount(FolderPath), SamplePath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where FileCount >= 25
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".candy"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), FileCount=dcount(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| where FileCount >= 25
| order by FirstSeen desc

    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-7810 ORB C2 relay connection to LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts internal hosts or edge devices communicating with the four UAT-7810 command-and-control / relay IPs on their distinctive non-standard ports (8088, 2222, 99). These IPs host the LONGLEASH intermediate C2 relay and DOGLEASH backdoor infrastructure used to build the China-nexus ORB proxy network. Rationale: Anchored on the four exact C2/relay IPs (194.233.92.26, 217.15.160.247, 217.15.164.147, 95.182.100.231) and their distinctive ports 8088/2222/99 pulled from the Talos UAT-7810 blog and confirmed by The Hacker News and BleepingComputer write-ups. Direct-IP IOC match on dedicated malicious infrastructure is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/china-linked-uat-7810-expands-orb.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1571 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM deliberately reaching the IPs during analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment or scanning tooling actively probing the IOC IPs
  • IP re-provisioned to a benign tenant after takedown (validate against current WHOIS/passive DNS)
  • Security researcher pivoting on the infrastructure from a corporate host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source host/device and process making the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName); confirm the IP is still attributed to UAT-7810 via passive DNS and the TLS cert fingerprint c2ab9adaba93ff094b8f3fc37d906014d870582039d276b7bd03e6fd583d8a15 / subject DN 'CN=exploit'. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source host/edge device, and capture volatile network state. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH hashes (see hash UC), inspect internet-facing Ruckus/ASUS routers for the /forms/doLogin exploit, and search for proxied traffic patterns (traffic in from one external peer, out to a different external peer) indicating ORB relay use.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-7810 Ruckus router RCE via /forms/doLogin command injection (CVE-2023-25717) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP GET/POST requests to the Ruckus Wireless Admin /forms/doLogin endpoint containing shell metacharacters in the credential parameters — the unauthenticated command-injection vector (CVE-2023-25717) UAT-7810 uses for initial access into edge devices before deploying DOGLEASH. Also flags requests from the campaign's known exploitation source IPs. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE-2023-25717 exploitation endpoint /forms/doLogin (confirmed via NVD/SentinelOne CVE records) combined with a shell-metacharacter regex targeting the command-injection payload, plus the campaign's known exploitation source IPs. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty because router HTTP request logs are not shipped to endpoint EDR or the standard Datadog sources — this detection lives in web/proxy/WAF telemetry (Splunk Web DM, Sentinel CommonSecurityLog). Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-25717 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2023-25717/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing the doLogin endpoint
  • Penetration test or red-team validation of the Ruckus CVE
  • Legitimate admin login to Ruckus Wireless Admin (no metacharacters — regex should exclude these)
  • Automated config/monitoring tooling hitting the router login page
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nmap","masscan","Nuclei") and SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8 sanctioned scanner ranges")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the RequestURL, confirm shell metacharacters are inside the username/password parameters (true injection vs. benign login), and check the target device is an internet-facing Ruckus/ASUS router at a vulnerable firmware. 2) Contain: block the source IP, take the exposed router off the internet or apply the vendor patch, and reset device credentials. 3) Hunt: on the router and any adjacent Linux hosts search for DOGLEASH command-execution artifacts (/bin/sh -c spawned by the web process) and outbound connections to the four ORB C2 IPs; confirm patch status of all Ruckus (CVE-2020-22653/22658/25717) and ASUS AiCloud (CVE-2025-2492) devices.
CommonSecurityLog

| where RequestURL has "/forms/doLogin"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"[;|`&$><]|%3B|%7C|%60|%24|%26|%3E"
    or SourceIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| where not(RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nmap","masscan","Nuclei"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-7810 LONGLEASH / DOGLEASH / JARLEASH backdoor binaries by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on file creation or process execution matching the confirmed SHA256 hashes of UAT-7810's LONGLEASH (upgraded SHORTLEASH) reverse-shell/proxy implant, the C-based DOGLEASH backdoor, the JARLEASH Java admin backdoor, and the LEASHTEST MIPS test binary. High-fidelity hash IOC match for the persistence/implant stage on any Linux staging server or router with EDR coverage. Rationale: Uses the exact SHA256 hashes for LONGLEASH (755fcee...), LEASHTEST (1b5649b...), JARLEASH (324d950..., bafba44...) and representative DOGLEASH variants (604b53f..., c92541f...) pulled from the Talos UAT-7810 IOC list. Exact-hash match is the highest-fidelity endpoint signal; Datadog/CloudWatch left empty as file-hash telemetry for these Linux implants isn't in those standard sources. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/china-linked-uat-7810-expands-orb.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst holding the samples on an instrumented workstation
  • EDR/AV quarantine or backup copy retaining the file (ActionType shows quarantine path)
  • Threat-intel sample-sharing repository synced to a corporate host
  • IR responder copying the artifact during an active investigation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash match and whether it is a live implant vs. an analyst/quarantine copy (check FolderPath/ActingProcessName and whether the process actually executed). 2) Contain: isolate the host/edge device, kill the running backdoor process, and preserve the binary for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host for outbound connections to the four ORB C2 IPs (ports 8088/2222/99), DOGLEASH '/bin/sh -c' child processes, JARLEASH FTP/SFTP/Netcat listeners, and JARLEASH startup script/config hashes; sweep all Linux staging servers and edge devices for the full DOGLEASH hash set.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm 12 Disables Install Scripts by Default to Reduce Supply Chain Risk

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has officially announced the release of npm version 12 with install scripts disabled by default, along with deprecating granular access tokens (GATs) designed to bypass two-factor authentication (2FA). The Microsoft-owned subsidiary noted that the following npm install behaviors that used to run automatically before have been made opt-in&nbsp;- allowScripts defaults to off, meaning

Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry

AikidoStepSecurity
2026-07-09 10 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to slip a backdoor into a widely used software development kit for the Injective blockchain. Disguised as harmless analytics, the code quietly captured wallet recovery phrases and private keys and sent them to an attacker-controlled server the moment a wallet was created or loaded. Automatic publishing pushed the tainted code out to 18 related packages within minutes, and it stayed live for less than an hour before being pulled and fixed. If your application installed any of the affected packages during that window, or pic…

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/network activity to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network, the character-code-rebuilt exfil host used by the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 to smuggle base64 wallet key material inside an X-Request-Id header disguised as gRPC-web traffic. Article-specific because the FQDN is a fixed IOC unique to this campaign. Rationale: The exfil FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is a fixed, campaign-unique IOC (a lookalike subdomain never served by real Injective infra); matching it exactly avoids the FP risk of the parent injective.network.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1132.001 T1041 T1001.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate future Injective testnet archival endpoint being stood up under this exact FQDN (verify DNS/PKI ownership)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the malicious package intentionally
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or research VM deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Internal DNS logging replaying old cached queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving host ran an @injectivelabs-dependent app; capture the initiating process (node.exe) and user. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat every wallet mnemonic/private key derived on it as exposed — freeze/rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts querying the FQDN, pull package-lock/yarn.lock for @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21, and search DeviceFileEvents for the two malicious build artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk AIInstallation Medium
Detects the two poisoned build files (accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) from @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 landing on disk, matched on their exact SHA-256 hashes. High fidelity IOC match that survives file renaming. Rationale: Both SHA-256 values are published IOCs for the exact malicious build artifacts; a hash match is unambiguous and near-zero FP, catching the stealer even if the file is renamed during transitive install.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / malware analyst intentionally storing the sample
  • Backup or EDR quarantine copy of the artifact triggering a second file event
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion writing the IOC file to a sandbox share
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and host; confirm whether it is a dev/CI machine or an analyst sandbox. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the affected node_modules, and pin @injectivelabs/* to a clean version (>=1.20.23); treat any wallet keys handled on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints/CI runners for the same hashes and for outbound contact to the exfil FQDN.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Structural supply-chain detection: the campaign-unique build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js appearing under a node_modules/@injectivelabs path. Resilient to re-signing/re-hash because it keys on the version-marker filenames + package scope rather than the SHA-256, catching victims who pulled the stealer transitively via any of the 18 sibling packages. Rationale: The build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js are unique to the poisoned 1.20.21 dist and act as a version marker; combined with the node_modules/@injectivelabs scope this flags transitive victims (e.g. via wallet-core) who never named sdk-ts directly, and survives re-hash of the still-downloadable deprecated package.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Aikido/other scanner replaying the artifact during a rescan
  • Developer intentionally checking out the compromised version to reproduce/analyze
  • A future clean @injectivelabs build coincidentally reusing the same hashed chunk name (unlikely — Rollup chunk hashes are content-derived)
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read the package's package.json version and lockfile to confirm 1.20.21 was resolved (directly or transitively). 2) Contain: delete node_modules, repin @injectivelabs/* to >=1.20.23, and rebuild; flag any wallet keys/seed phrases derived on the host for rotation. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/CI job with @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21 in lockfiles and correlate hosts against exfil-domain contacts and the SHA-256 file detection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "injectivelabs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "injectivelabs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process

status: experimental
description: |

            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'

            - '\Exodus.exe'

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("01219285b16ce85c70cdf47a71a551ff5e41f1ed", "fd105db9073a21a3b58d5bd32622204ec8b57993", "5486f13e799d9c90095c5f581a04ad867d768f66", "7c4b1a092d8cbbcda469bda5a88db2a742d15b4a") or SHA1 in~ ("01219285b16ce85c70cdf47a71a551ff5e41f1ed", "fd105db9073a21a3b58d5bd32622204ec8b57993", "5486f13e799d9c90095c5f581a04ad867d768f66", "7c4b1a092d8cbbcda469bda5a88db2a742d15b4a") or MD5 in~ ("01219285b16ce85c70cdf47a71a551ff5e41f1ed", "fd105db9073a21a3b58d5bd32622204ec8b57993", "5486f13e799d9c90095c5f581a04ad867d768f66", "7c4b1a092d8cbbcda469bda5a88db2a742d15b4a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("01219285b16ce85c70cdf47a71a551ff5e41f1ed", "fd105db9073a21a3b58d5bd32622204ec8b57993", "5486f13e799d9c90095c5f581a04ad867d768f66", "7c4b1a092d8cbbcda469bda5a88db2a742d15b4a") or SHA1 in~ ("01219285b16ce85c70cdf47a71a551ff5e41f1ed", "fd105db9073a21a3b58d5bd32622204ec8b57993", "5486f13e799d9c90095c5f581a04ad867d768f66", "7c4b1a092d8cbbcda469bda5a88db2a742d15b4a") or MD5 in~ ("01219285b16ce85c70cdf47a71a551ff5e41f1ed", "fd105db9073a21a3b58d5bd32622204ec8b57993", "5486f13e799d9c90095c5f581a04ad867d768f66", "7c4b1a092d8cbbcda469bda5a88db2a742d15b4a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["01219285b16ce85c70cdf47a71a551ff5e41f1ed", "fd105db9073a21a3b58d5bd32622204ec8b57993", "5486f13e799d9c90095c5f581a04ad867d768f66", "7c4b1a092d8cbbcda469bda5a88db2a742d15b4a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ThreatsDay: Cloud Bucket Hijacking, Windows LPE Chain, Global Fraud Bust + 17 More Stories

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 24 use cases 12 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Most security mess starts as admin work. A link gets clicked. A tool gets trusted. A bucket name gets reused. A setting stays loose because nobody wants to touch&nbsp;it. This week is full of that kind of damage. Not loud. Not clever. Just small gaps doing big jobs. The worst part is how normal it all looks until the bill arrives. The full ThreatsDay list is below.
