Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EtherRAT delivery: cmd.exe → curl.exe fetching v7.msi from camorreado.click · [LLM] Teams-lure RMM install: HopToDesk + AnyDesk launched from Teams/browser · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Esri ArcGIS Server CVE-2026-9181 path traversal in REST Uploads resource · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Cloud Bucket Hijacking, Windows LPE Chain, Global Fraud Bust + 17 Mo
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] EtherRAT loader: msiexec runs v7.msi then node.exe executes staged JS runtime · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Payment-SDK typosquat exfil: node/python egress to *.ngrok-free.dev from build host · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
EtherRAT delivery: cmd.exe → curl.exe fetching v7.msi from camorreado.click AIDelivery High
Hunts the Unit 42 EtherRAT delivery step where a fake Teams 'System Administrator' guides the victim to run cmd.exe which shells out to curl.exe to download a malicious MSI (v7.msi, one of v1–v9) from camorreado[.]click. Anchored on the specific staging domain and the curl-downloads-MSI chain. Rationale: camorreado[.]click and v7.msi are named in the article and confirmed by BleepingComputer/gbhackers write-ups of the same Unit 42 EtherRAT campaign; curl.exe fetching an MSI from that domain is a single high-fidelity chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-it-support-calls-on-microsoft-teams-push-etherrat-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-abuse-cross-tenant-teams-chat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.003 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin using curl in cmd to pull a legit vendor MSI over HTTP
  • Software packaging/CI scripts that fetch MSIs via curl
  • Chocolatey/winget wrappers shelling out to curl
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chocolatey","winget","packer") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and confirm the URL is camorreado[.]click or another vX.msi path; capture the downloaded MSI hash and the parent cmd/Teams context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block camorreado[.]click at proxy/DNS, kill msiexec/node child processes, and revoke the user's active sessions. 3) Hunt: search the estate for HopToDesk.exe/AnyDesk.exe installs, node.exe spawned by msiexec, and outbound Ethereum RPC / secondary C2 from the same hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "camorreado.click" or ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "camorreado.click" or ProcessCommandLine has "v7.msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine has "v7.msi"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: EtherRAT MSI download via curl from camorreado.click
id: 7f3c2a1e-9b4d-4c8a-b2e1-3f5a6d7c8e90
description: Detects cmd/powershell spawning curl to download an MSI from the EtherRAT staging domain camorreado.click
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-cloud-bucket-hijacking.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-it-support-calls-on-microsoft-teams-push-etherrat-malware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'camorreado.click'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\Curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*camorreado.click* OR *v7.msi*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\curl\.exe$/i
| regex("camorreado\.click", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process=*camorreado.click* OR Processes.process=*v7.msi* OR Processes.process=*.msi*) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process=*camorreado.click* OR process=*.msi* | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process=*camorreado.click* OR Processes.process=*v7.msi* OR Processes.process=*.msi*) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process=*camorreado.click* OR process=*.msi* | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
EtherRAT loader: msiexec runs v7.msi then node.exe executes staged JS runtime AIInstallation High
Hunts the second EtherRAT stage where msiexec executes the malicious MSI (v7.msi), which drops a legitimate Node.js runtime (v18.20.5) into a renamed directory and launches node.exe against an obfuscated JavaScript loader. Anchored on msiexec referencing the staging artefact and node.exe being spawned by msiexec/cmd from a user-writable path. Rationale: Unit 42 (corroborated by BleepingComputer) documents v7.msi staging Node.js v18.20.5 and running an obfuscated JS loader; node.exe parented by msiexec.exe from a temp/appdata path is a rare, campaign-specific chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-it-support-calls-on-microsoft-teams-push-etherrat-malware/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-leverage-microsoft-teams-call/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit Node-based desktop apps (some Electron installers) launching node.exe from an MSI
  • Enterprise app packaging that bundles a private Node runtime via MSI
  • Developer toolchains invoking node from a temp build directory
  • VS Code / npm-installed global tools running node from AppData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Code.exe","electron","nvm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the MSI product/source is v#.msi from camorreado[.]click and inspect the node.exe command line and the JS file it points at (renamed runtime dir is a tell). 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate node.exe and msiexec children, quarantine the MSI and dropped runtime folder. 3) Hunt: look for Ethereum JSON-RPC / smart-contract lookups and secondary C2 egress from node.exe, plus HopToDesk/AnyDesk persistence on the same and peer hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "msiexec.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("camorreado.click","v7.msi"))
    or (FileName =~ "node.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","cmd.exe") and FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe" and (CommandLine has "camorreado.click" or CommandLine has "v7.msi"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" and ParentProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MsiExec.exe OR *\\MSIEXEC.EXE) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/msiexec\.exe/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=msiexec.exe AND (Processes.process=*camorreado.click* OR Processes.process=*v7.msi*)) OR (Processes.process_name=node.exe AND Processes.parent_process_name=msiexec.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=msiexec.exe AND (Processes.process=*camorreado.click* OR Processes.process=*v7.msi*)) OR (Processes.process_name=node.exe AND Processes.parent_process_name=msiexec.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Teams-lure RMM install: HopToDesk + AnyDesk launched from Teams/browser AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the EtherRAT initial-access step where an actor impersonating a 'System Administrator' over a Microsoft Teams call abuses give/request control and directs the victim to install HopToDesk and AnyDesk for persistence. Anchored on these two specific RMM binaries executing with a Teams or browser parent. Rationale: Article and Register/CyberSecurityNews coverage name HopToDesk and AnyDesk as the RMM tools pushed via the Teams give/request-control lure; requiring a Teams/browser parent filters routine sanctioned RMM usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/07/fake-it-bods-on-microsoft-teams-coax-workers-into-installing-malware/5267610 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-leverage-microsoft-teams-call/
ATT&CKT1219 T1656 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit helpdesk that genuinely uses AnyDesk and instructs users to download it during a Teams call
  • End user installing HopToDesk/AnyDesk for personal remote access
  • MSP onboarding pushing AnyDesk via a browser download
  • AnyDesk auto-update relaunching itself (parent would be AnyDesk, filtered out)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","HopToDesk.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify whether the RMM install correlates with an inbound external/cross-tenant Teams call and an 'Employee Survey' phishing email to the same user; check if HopToDesk (uncommon in enterprise) is present. 2) Contain: uninstall the RMM tools, block their update/relay domains, isolate the host, and reset the user's credentials/sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot to curl→v7.msi and node.exe-from-msiexec activity on the host and check Teams admin logs for external control grants across other users.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("HopToDesk.exe","AnyDesk.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ms-teams.exe","Teams.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\HopToDesk.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\AnyDesk.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ms-teams.exe","Teams.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Payment-SDK typosquat exfil: node/python egress to *.ngrok-free.dev from build host AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Socket-reported npm/PyPI typosquat campaign against Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller SDKs, which harvests developer secrets and tunnels them to an Ngrok endpoint (caliber-spinner-finishing[.]ngrok-free.dev). Anchored on package-manager/runtime processes (node/npm/python/pip) resolving or connecting to an ngrok-free.dev host. Rationale: Socket's write-up (corroborating THN) names caliber-spinner-finishing[.]ngrok-free.dev as the exfil endpoint; ngrok-free.dev egress initiated by a package manager/runtime on a build host is high-signal for supply-chain secret theft. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/npm-pypi-campaign-typosquats-popular-secure-payment-apps • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-paysafe-skrill-sdks-on-npm-and-pypi-steal-credentials/
ATT&CKT1567 T1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using an ngrok tunnel to expose a local dev server
  • QA/webhook testing tools that resolve ngrok-free.dev
  • Node app with an ngrok SDK dependency used intentionally
  • Security researcher analysing the sample in a monitored VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ngrok" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--tunnel"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating node/npm/python process, capture its command line and the package installed just before the connection, and confirm the destination host (caliber-spinner-finishing[.]ngrok-free.dev). 2) Contain: block *.ngrok-free.dev at egress for build/CI segments, rotate any KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASS/AUTH/API env-var secrets present on the host, and remove the offending npm/PyPI package. 3) Hunt: search package-lock/requirements history for the 17 typosquatted Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller packages across all developer and CI hosts and review outbound to newly-seen ngrok subdomains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "ngrok-free.dev" or RemoteUrl has "caliber-spinner-finishing"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "ngrok-free.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Esri ArcGIS Server CVE-2026-9181 path traversal in REST Uploads resource AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-9181 (CVSS 9.8) in Esri ArcGIS Server ≤12.0, where crafted path parameters to the ArcGIS Server REST Uploads resource traverse outside the intended directory to read sensitive files. Anchored on web requests to the arcgis REST path containing directory-traversal sequences. Rationale: Article cites CVE-2026-9181 in the ArcGIS Server REST Uploads resource exploited via crafted path parameters (Horizon3.ai); traversal tokens (../, %2e%2e) against an arcgis REST/uploads URI is the concrete exploit signature. No Defender/Falcon/Datadog telemetry surfaces raw web-request URIs in this tenant, so those fields are left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-cloud-bucket-hijacking.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ArcGIS map service URLs that legitimately contain '..' in a layer/query string
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualus) probing ArcGIS endpoints
  • Encoded but benign relative paths in ArcGIS REST query parameters
  • Internal pentest/red-team validating the patch
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and the request returned 200/206 with an anomalous file path; check ArcGIS Server version against the ≤12.0 vulnerable range. 2) Contain: virtual-patch/WAF the REST Uploads endpoint, restrict it to authenticated access, and apply Esri's fixed build; block the offending source IP. 3) Hunt: review all successful traversal responses for which files were read (config, keystores, tokens), rotate exposed secrets, and correlate the source IP with follow-on auth or webshell-drop attempts.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has "arcgis"
| where csUriStem has "upload" or csUriStem has "rest"
| where csUriStem has_any ("..","%2e%2e","..%2f","%2e%2e%2f") or csUriQuery has_any ("..","%2e%2e","..%2f","%2e%2e%2f")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-9181", "CVE-2025-49760", "CVE-2025-59200", "CVE-2022-25477", "CVE-2022-25478", "CVE-2022-25479", "CVE-2022-25480", "CVE-2024-40431", "CVE-2024-40432")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.

Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)

            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the

SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82") or SHA1 in~ ("fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82") or MD5 in~ ("fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82") or SHA1 in~ ("fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82") or MD5 in~ ("fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("fc2907fa866f86e0821f75060a331ce69ee10ff3aa374587993b17ba5406fa33", "c2eeb74892408496f5a307a5b1fdc92d94fd014ab4252868f04046bf84718ab6", "94cb54d53927e4ba469099760db531be563a84d716df69e864062d90f0f2448d", "0cb2f7651d50e1ed1a691e82f0297d49444bdded2461e136cffb156d4f234e52", "c16784e2c7b3e3b798addd718850da18f8eb532ab8f352c769a4470d7124805d", "d46b4e8d188fe1773c44d38d730dcb6287639568240c765d9ad4ad79cd239e82")

GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-09 16 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

GigaWiper, also tracked as BLUERABBIT, is a destructive backdoor that combines multiple wiping and ransomware-like capabilities into a single operational platform. This blog analyzes how the malware incorporates code from several previously separate malware families and provides guidance to help defenders detect and defend against similar threats. The post GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1047 T1053.005 T1059.001 T1190 T1486 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GigaWiper persistence: 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task run-every-minute · [LLM] GigaWiper persistence marker: HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment counter · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GigaWiper C2: RabbitMQ/Redis connection to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GigaWiper destructive Golang backdoor/wiper by known SHA-256 · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GigaWiper destructive Golang backdoor/wiper by known SHA-256 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution, drop, or load of the five Microsoft-published GigaWiper backdoor and standalone-wiper binaries. High-fidelity because these hashes are the destructive tooling itself (raw-disk wipe, Crucio-derived fake ransomware, FlockWiper re-implementation) - a single hit is an active destruction event. Rationale: Uses the five exact SHA-256 IOCs Microsoft published (Table 2) for the GigaWiper backdoor and standalone wiper; a hash match is unambiguous destructive tooling. Architecture corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT (same RabbitMQ+Redis+dual-wiper design). Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/the-anatomy-of-wiper-malware-part-1/
ATT&CKT1485 T1561.002 T1561.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or IR team detonating a sample in a lab that reports to the same tenant
  • Threat-intel/EDR test harness deliberately dropping the IOC hashes to validate detections
  • Security vendor scan uploading the sample to a scanning appliance on the network
  • Re-hash collision is not credible for SHA-256, so genuine benign hits are near-zero
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malwarelab","detonation") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cuckoo.exe","procdump.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the hash match and check DeviceProcessEvents for the process tree and whether WipeMain / schtasks 'OneDrive Update' / connections to 185.182.193.21 already followed - if any did, treat as live destruction, not a scan. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately network-isolate the host via Defender, force-block the five hashes tenant-wide, and snapshot/preserve any still-intact disks before the wiper reboots them. 3) HUNT: Sweep the tenant for the other four hashes, the 'OneDrive Update' task, HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment, and outbound traffic to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 to find other beachheads before the fanout 'All' exchange broadcasts a wipe command.

GigaWiper persistence: 'OneDrive Update' scheduled task run-every-minute AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of GigaWiper's persistence task, a schtasks invocation that registers a task literally named 'OneDrive Update' scheduled to run every minute plus at startup. Article-specific: real OneDrive uses tasks named 'OneDrive Standalone Update Task' under OneDrive.exe, never a per-minute 'OneDrive Update'. Rationale: Pins on the exact task name 'OneDrive Update' plus the per-minute schedule from the article's Figure 3 persistence command, and excludes genuine OneDrive updater parents - the masquerade name is the high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal software-distribution or RMM tool that names a custom task 'OneDrive Update' (rare; usually branded to the vendor)
  • Admin manually recreating a broken OneDrive updater task with a non-standard name
  • GPO/Intune deployment scripting a OneDrive keep-alive task per minute (should originate from a known deployment parent - allowlist it)
  • Backup/monitoring agent creating a minute-cadence task with 'OneDrive' in the name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\OneDrive"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the task XML (schtasks /query /tn 'OneDrive Update' /xml) and the InitiatingProcess hash - if the action points to an unsigned Golang PE or a non-OneDrive path, escalate. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the task (schtasks /delete /tn 'OneDrive Update' /f), isolate the host, and block the initiating binary's hash. 3) HUNT: Check HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment execution-counter value on this and peer hosts, and query for the five GigaWiper hashes and 185.182.193.21 connections to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("/create", "OneDrive Update")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sc minute", "/sc onstart", "minute")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe", "msiexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("/create", "OneDrive Update")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/sc minute", "/sc onstart", "minute")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith "\\OneDrive.exe" and ParentProcessName !endswith "\\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GigaWiper C2: RabbitMQ/Redis connection to 185.182.193.21:5544/7542 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to GigaWiper's hard-coded C2 host 185.182.193.21 on the RabbitMQ (AMQP 5544) and Redis (7542) ports it uses for command receipt and result upload. Article-specific: workstation processes speaking AMQP/Redis to a public IP on these non-standard ports is the backdoor's C2 heartbeat. Rationale: Uses Microsoft's exact hard-coded C2 IP 185.182.193.21 (ports 5544 RabbitMQ / 7542 Redis). The RabbitMQ-tasking + Redis-state design is independently corroborated by Binary Defense's BLUERABBIT, raising confidence in the pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1071 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst or sinkhole researcher intentionally probing 185.182.193.21 from a monitored host
  • Firewall/IDS appliance sourcing a block-verification connection to the IOC IP
  • Shared-hosting reuse: the IP is later reassigned to a benign service (validate WHOIS/passive-DNS before trusting a stale IOC)
  • Legitimate internal RabbitMQ/Redis on a different IP is unaffected - this pins the specific malicious IP, not the ports alone
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify InitiatingProcess/ContextImageFileName making the connection - an unsigned Golang PE or a process also matching the GigaWiper hashes confirms C2. 2) CONTAIN: Block 185.182.193.21 at the firewall/EDR, isolate the beaconing host, and preserve memory before reboot (the wiper forces an immediate restart). 3) HUNT: Because commands publish to the fanout 'All' exchange (broadcast to every infected client), assume multiple hosts - sweep the tenant for any traffic to 185.182.193.21, the 'OneDrive Update' task, and the five GigaWiper hashes to enumerate all bots before a wipe is issued.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "185.182.193.21"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "185.182.193.21"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GigaWiper persistence marker: HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment counter AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes to GigaWiper's execution-count registry value under HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment by a process that is not the genuine OneDrive client. Article-specific: real OneDrive stores state under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive, so a bare SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment key is a masqueraded first-run/run-count marker. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masqueraded persistence key HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment from the article, excluding genuine OneDrive writers - distinct from the real HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive path, so hits are high-fidelity. Falcon left empty: this non-ASEP HKCU value is not carried by FDR's AsepValueUpdate autostart telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://binarydefense.com/resources/blog/bluerabbit-a-golang-based-backdoor-with-ransomware-and-destructive-capabilities
ATT&CKT1112 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party OneDrive management/backup utility that writes state under a non-Microsoft OneDrive key
  • Legacy or renamed OneDrive build writing to SOFTWARE\OneDrive rather than SOFTWARE\Microsoft\OneDrive
  • Admin/registry-cleanup tooling touching an orphaned OneDrive key during troubleshooting
  • Endpoint-management agent snapshotting HKCU hives and re-writing values (writer would be the agent, not a Golang PE)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft OneDrive\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the value data (it should be a small integer run-counter) and the writing process hash - correlate against the GigaWiper hash list and the 'OneDrive Update' task on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: If the writer is unsigned/Golang or hash-matched, isolate the host, delete the key, remove the task, and block the binary. 3) HUNT: The key is set to '0' on first run and incremented each scheduled execution - hosts with value > 0 have run repeatedly; pivot on those plus 185.182.193.21 traffic to find long-dwell infections.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment"
| where ActingProcessName !has "OneDrive.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or SHA1 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd") or MD5 in~ ("633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["633d4cbd496b1094495da89a64f5e6c31a0f6d4d1488411db5b0cba1cfe42001", "ce9ad5f6c12019f4aae5b189bd8ddf5bb09e75b06a0a587b25a855c65948c913", "f622ed85ef31ad4ab973f4e74524866fe1bb44f0965ad2b2ad796cd657a05bfd", "9706a192e2c1a1faaf0a521daf31c2af60ff4590e3f47bbb4abc227f42af0683", "3c30deb6556a94cfb84ae51798f4aecfae8c7358e55fdb321c5f2376579631cd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — One Target, Two Flags | Rival Espionage Actors Converge On Pakistani Law Enforce
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement · [LLM] Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement AICommand & Control High
Hunts any internal host establishing outbound connections to the 13 C2 IPs SentinelLABS attributed to the four tooling clusters (PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, Remcos) converging on Balochistan Police and other Pakistani law-enforcement orgs between Feb 2024 and Apr 2026. Pure network-IOC match on disclosed espionage C2 servers. Rationale: Anchored on the exact 13 C2 IPs from Table 1 / code blocks (PlugX 172.111.233.x + 172.94.9.x + 45.74.6.17, ShadowPad 45.125.32.218, Cobalt Strike 142.171.183.8 + 193.42.25.65, Remcos 89.31.121.220). Any egress to these known-bad hosts is high-fidelity; the tooling families and Pakistani-entity victimology are corroborated externally, though the specific IPs are from the SentinelLABS primary report only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad • https://thehackernews.com/2023/07/pakistani-entities-targeted-in.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately sandboxing or sinkholing one of these IPs from a corporate host
  • IP reassignment after takedown — a benign service later hosted on a recycled VPS IP (172.94.9.x / 45.x hosting ranges are commodity VPS)
  • Internal threat-intel validation tooling or EDR connectivity checks pinging the IOC list
  • Proxy/NAT concentration causing many internal hosts to appear as one src toward the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR/AV connectivity-check processes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection is genuinely outbound and established (not a blocked/attempt), identify the initiating process and host role — servers hosting the CMS/FIR/HRMIS/HotelEye/CRMS apps are highest priority. 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at perimeter, isolate the host, snapshot memory before reboot to preserve PlugX/ShadowPad in-memory implants. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DLL side-loading (unsigned DLL next to a signed EXE), scheduled tasks/Run keys created near first-seen, and lateral SMB/RDP from the host; sweep the org for any other host touching the same /24s (172.111.233.0/24, 172.94.9.0/24).

| where RemoteIP in (C2)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc

Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) AICommand & Control Medium
Tighter server-side pivot: a web/application-server process (IIS w3wp, Apache/Tomcat java, nginx, php-cgi) on a Pakistani law-enforcement web server initiating outbound to the disclosed C2 IPs. Grounds on the article's China-nexus 'custom implants masquerading as a portal update' planted in one of the citizen/police web applications (e.g. the Complaint Management System). Rationale: Combines the exact C2 IP set with a server-process filter to isolate the article's specific scenario — a China-nexus implant planted in a citizen/police web application (CMS) beaconing out. Web-server processes reaching commodity-VPS C2 IPs is extremely rare and high-fidelity, and directly targets the compromised-webapp vector the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1505.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately calling an outbound API that happens to be on a recycled VPS IP after IOC takedown
  • Java-based agent/monitoring on the web server making outbound telemetry calls
  • Server-side update/package fetch (Tomcat/Maven, php composer) to a mirror on the same hosting range
  • App-server health-check or CDN origin-pull to a reassigned address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "maven" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "composer" // exclude server package-manager fetches
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which web application the process serves (CMS/FIR/HRMIS/AVLS/HotelEye/CRMS) and whether the beacon started after a recent 'portal update'/deployment window; review web-root for recently modified/added handler, JSP, ASPX or PHP files. 2) Contain: take the web app offline or block egress, preserve IIS/Tomcat logs and web-root for forensics, rotate app/service and DB credentials the server can reach. 3) Hunt: search web access logs (W3CIISLog/AppServiceHTTPLogs) for the implant's request pattern, look for webshell-style POSTs, and pivot to any DB export or biometric/criminal-record access from the compromised app identity.

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

AI has changed how fast attacks move. Work that once took an attacker days now takes minutes. Using models like Mythos, attackers write tailored bait, pick targets, test what lands, and jump to the next host before your team clears the first alert. That is the gap, and it is not your fault. The tools and runbooks most teams run on were built for attackers who work at human speed. AI-driven
